Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Qian et al use a very interesting and largely novel approach to address whether phenotypes in extant lineages have been established by selection or neutral drift. They argue that if a phenotype has been established through a selective process, then evolved changes to that phenotype, under strictly neutral evolution, would tend to more often reverse than reinforce it. The logic is neat: random changes to an already optimized trait would be expected to more often impair than further improve it, whereas changes to a neutral trait would be random in direction.
They employ this logic to a yeast model strain, S388c, and test whether its capacity to respond to stressful environments, exemplified by exposure to moderate amounts of either NaCl or the antifungal clotrimazole, through changes to transcript abundance, is systematically lost or not when the strain is evolved neutrally.
They find that, somewhat surprisingly, there are no directional evolutionary changes to the transcriptional response to NaCl, implying that it is neutral, but that evolutionary changes to clotrimazole transcriptional plasticity are directional and tend to reverse it, implying that it has been selectively favoured.
I very much appreciate the fundamental thinking in this paper, which I find refreshing, sound and employable on a broad scale, to a range of microbial phenotypes. As such, I think it has the potential to be well cited, and I can see contexts in which I would cite it. The data are mostly analysed in a correct and careful way, and the clotrimazole results seems clear.
Unfortunately, I am not entirely convinced about the conclusions, because of various design issues, and would like to see additional follow-up analysis before I am ready to accept the claim of selection.
Major concerns:
1. Looking for natural selection for clotrimazole plasticity in a S288c derivative doesn’t make much evolutionary sense. First, S288c is an artificial hybrid, whose genetic variants never jointly have been exposed to any selection outside the laboratory. S288c also tends to be a phenotypic outlier (see e.g.https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgen.1002111). This can also be seen in Fig 1E for YPD and NaCl, which calls for caution in interpretations of YPD and NaCl responses.
Response: The reviewer is correct that S288c is a hybrid strain that created in the lab.
However, its parental strains are all natural strains that have evolved under natural condition. As such, the alleles present in S288c have indeed undergone natural selection prior to the hybridization, which provides valuable evolutionary context.
The fact that S288c may appear as a genotypic outlier compared to other strains is likely a result of its frequent cultivation in laboratory environments like YPD and SC, which could have led to it acquiring higher fitness under these specific conditions. Finally, we selected the BY4741 background because it is one of the most widely used model strains in yeast genetics and genomics, with extensive genomic, transcriptomic, and functional resources available. This choice ensures experimental reproducibility and facilitates comparisons with prior studies investigating gene expression plasticity and mutation accumulation in yeast.
Second, clotrimazole, as other azoles of its class, is a synthetic compound. Although some azoles have very recently begun to be used as fungicides in agriculture, this short period could hardly have selected for an optimal clotrimazole transcriptional response even in natural yeast. With both these points in mind, I find it hard to understand how natural selection could have worked to achieve optimal S288c transcriptional responses to clotrimazole. This would presumably require many genetic variants being driven to high frequencies - and their beneficial combinations not having been disrupted by the process creating S288. It would have been far easier to argue for natural selection for plasticity under NaCl exposure (see below). And ideally, experiments would have been performed with a wild yeast strain and exposure omnipresent natural selection pressures, such as nitrogen limitation, a respiratory carbon source, or temperature. As is, I am left with strong doubts. The reduced clotrimazole expression plasticity in MA lines seems robust. But, either this plasticity was established by selection pressures other than azoles. Or, they are not reflective of selection at all. This needs to be resolved and discussed. Could the plastic changes observed simply be a consequence of MA strains growing at a different rate? Or - of MA strains not being in the same mid-log phase when harvested as the progenitor, but one of the two approaching the end of log-phase growth which has entirely different expression patterns? If cells are not in comparable physiological states, we would be looking at a technical artefact, not selection? At a minimum, we should be shown log-scale growth curves with points of harvest indicated, ideally with 1st derivatives included, to demonstrate that cells are in comparable, mid-log states. A comparison of observed plasticities to that of previous studies looking at how BY transcript abundance changes as a function of growth phase could also help reject the explanation of cultures being in different growth states. If technical explanations to the observed difference can be rejected, I would be more ready to accept the claim of selection – but what would be the selection pressure, given that it is highly unlikely to have been azoles? Are we looking at a general stress response? The yeast “general stress response” is typically defined by distinct transcription changes in the initial shock phase after shift to a new environment, but there may be remnants of that also in the subsequent growth phase. Are we looking at a response to reduced/increased membrane stability/permeability? What would the driving selection pressure have been? There are extensive datasets on yeast transcriptional responses, and a very rich yeast literature, that could be used to illuminate this. At this stage, given that the authors have just one positive signal for an environment of dubious selective importance, and a negative signal for the environment that I would readily accept having been of selective importance, and this using a strain never exposed to natural selection, I feel the obligation to be cautious.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this very thoughtful and comprehensive comment. We have carefully considered each point and made several additions and clarifications in response.
1. Growth phase
We fully agree that differences in growth state could confound transcriptomic comparisons. To address this, we have now included a new Supplementary Figure 8 showing the complete growth curves for all strains under each experimental condition. As shown below, both the natural strains and MA lines were harvested at comparable mid-logarithmic growth phases (OD ≈ 0.4–0.6 after subtracting media OD), well
660
before the onset of stationary phase. Therefore, the transcriptional differences observed between conditions are unlikely to result from differences in growth phase..
Supplementary Figure 8. Growth curves and sampling windows for MA lines, natural strains, and the progenitor in the four environments. a–d, Growth curves of MA lines and the progenitor; e–h, growth curves of natural strains. The gray shaded areas indicate the sampling windows.
2. Evolutionary relevance of clotrimazole stress
We agree with the reviewer that clotrimazole, as a synthetic azole developed in the 1960s, does not represent a stressor that yeast would have encountered in its evolutionary history. We therefore consider clotrimazole to be a novel stressor, providing an opportunity to examine how yeast respond transcriptionally to completely unfamiliar chemical challenges.
To explore why yeast can still mount an apparently adaptive transcriptional response to clotrimazole, we analyzed DEGs between YPD and clotrimazole conditions. Among the genes whose expression was induced under clotrimazole, Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed significant overrepresentation of categories such as response to oxidative stress and response to chemical stimulus (Fisher’s exact test, P < 0.05 after BH correction). These categories were consistently enriched in natural strains but largely absent in MA lines. Previous studies have shown that oxidative stress response is broadly activated when yeast encounter diverse environmental challenges, while response to chemical stimulus encompasses reactions to a wide range of toxic or xenobiotic compounds, not limited to azoles.
These results strongly suggest that the transcriptional plasticity observed under clotrimazole treatment reflects activation of the general stress response rather than a clotrimazole-specific adaptation. Thus, although yeast have never experienced clotrimazole during their evolutionary history, they can still employ general stress-response pathways to mitigate the effects of such novel stressors. We have clarified this interpretation in the revised Discussion section, emphasizing that the observed adaptive plasticity likely stems from selection for general stress responsiveness.
3. Neutral plasticity under NaCl
To test whether the neutral pattern observed under NaCl stress was specific to that condition, we performed an additional experiment exposing yeast to heat stress (37 °C), a ubiquitous environmental challenge. The results were consistent with those under NaCl stress, showing a neutral pattern of expression plasticity.
We have added a new paragraph in the Discussion introducing the concept of genetic assimilation to explain this pattern. Genetic assimilation describes the evolutionary process by which an environmentally induced phenotype becomes genetically fixed, leading to a loss of plasticity over time. Under this model, stressors that are frequently encountered, such as NaCl or temperature fluctuations, are more likely to drive fixation of adaptive expression patterns, resulting in the neutral plasticity observed in our study.
In contrast, novel stressors like clotrimazole can still reveal adaptive plasticity, as their responses remain under active selection through general stress pathways.
Finally, we note that our analysis focuses on genome-wide patterns of plasticity; we cannot exclude the possibility that the plastic expression of specific genes under NaCl or heat stress remains adaptive. This clarification has been added to the Discussion section.
2. If the observed plasticities lost in MA lines are indeed beneficial in the progenitor - then fitness should be reduced in the neutrally evolved MA lines, relative the progenitor, in the relevant environments? In the absence of such a fitness loss, the arguments for selection appear circumstantial to me. Relevant environments would seem to be clotrimazole, even though it doesn’t make much evolutionary sense, or other commonly encountered environments that could induce very similar plastic changes. For example, the authors argue for the oxidative stress response component of the observed plasticity being selectively important. This could be tested, e.g. using hydrogenperoxide or paraquat. In the absence of data demonstrating that the loss of plasticity is accompanied by a loss of fitness, I find it hard to accept the selection argument. A competition experiment that competes several evolved MA lines individually against the progenitor in clotrimazole and e.g. paraquat, and that estimates the selection coefficient from frequency change, would at least associate plasticity loss to fitness loss, and growth data could potentially be used as well (see below). The really convincing experiment would be to identify and then engineer the causative plasticity loss mutations, only, in a WT and compete that against the WT to establish true causality between plasticity loss and fitness loss. As is, the inference of selection from MA line transcriptional change is too circumstantial for me, and would need confirmation by supporting data.
Response: We agree that demonstrating an association between the loss of expression plasticity and a corresponding fitness reduction would provide stronger support for selection acting on plasticity.
Following the reviewer’s recommendation, we conducted additional experiments to test whether the loss of plasticity observed in the MA lines is linked to decreased fitness in relevant environments. Specifically, because our results indicate that the oxidative stress response is a major component of the gene expression plasticity induced by clotrimazole, we reasoned that if this pathway is compromised by mutations accumulated during the MA process, then MA lines with lower fitness under clotrimazole should also show reduced fitness under oxidative stress.
To test this hypothesis, we measured the competitive fitness of all 15 MA lines in YPD media containing 1 μM clotrimazole and YPD media containing 0.1 mM hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). The results show a significant positive correlation between the fitness reductions (relative to YPD) across the two conditions (Pearson’s r = 0.62, P = 0.014; see new Supplementary Figure 5). This relationship suggests that the same biological mechanisms underlie the reduced fitness of MA lines in both environments.
Supplementary Figure 5. The correlation of fitness reduction of MA lines in hydrogen peroxide and clotrimazole. Fitness was measured by competitive growth assay. Each gray point represents a MA line. The black line shows the fitted linear regression, with the shaded area indicating the 95% confidence interval.
3. Growth data, such as reported in Fig 1D, could convince us that MA lines are less fit, in e.g. clotrimazole, than the BY progenitor – but this does not appear to be the case? However, we should be shown growth curves for the BY and the MA lines. It may be that a fitness defect is reflected in growth properties other than growth rates? I also have question marks around how the growth was estimated. Optical density and cell density are not linearly related, something that is normally accounted for either by dilution down to the near-linear range, or a post-experimental mathematical correction for the non-linearity (see e.g. https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12859-016-1134-2). Unless this was done, the estimated growth will be incorrect, which as outlined in point 1 and 2 could have serious implications. Fig 1D gives some cause for concern in that growth has been correctly analyzed. If what is shown here is the maximum specific growth rate, umax - and even more so if it is the average growth rate across the entire growth interval - values are unrealistically high. A umax of 0.35-0.45 in YPD is standard, a value of 0.8, as shown, would imply doubling times well below an hour, which is outside the realistic range.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these detailed and thoughtful comments regarding the growth-rate analysis and fitness interpretation. We confirm that, as shown in Figure 1D, the MA lines indeed exhibit lower fitness than the progenitor strain in the clotrimazole environment. We agree that growth rate is only one aspect of fitness and that other growth properties such as lag time, maximum growth rate during the logarithmic phase, and final yield can all contribute to overall fitness. In this study, we used maximum growth rate as a proxy for fitness, as it provides a robust and comparable measure of physiological performance across strains and conditions.
We agree that optical density (OD) and cell density are not linearly correlated. To address this issue, we established an OD–cell density calibration curve based on manual cell counts and applied this calibration to convert OD measurements to actual cell densities prior to growth-rate estimation. This step minimizes potential non-linearity artifacts.
Finally, we confirm that the reported growth-rate values represent maximum specific growth rates (μ ). To measure growth rate, OD was recorded every 20 minutes and
max
converted to cell density using the calibration curve. The slopes of ln (cell density) over time were computed for all overlapping 60-minute windows. To reduce the influence of transient fluctuations, the two highest slopes were discarded, and the mean of the third to eighth highest slopes was used to represent μ . We note that this value is
max
expressed per minute, and therefore a μ of 0.8 corresponds to approximately 0.8 ×
max
60 = 48% increase per hour, which falls within the biologically reasonable range for yeast growing in rich medium. This clarification has been added to the revised Methods section.
4. In paragraph 4, I feel that the division of evolved changes to plasticity into co-directional and reversed gives a too low degree of resolution. “Repressions turning into inductions” are in this classification grouped together with “inductions turning into repressions”, which does not make much biological sense. Moreover, potential trends of inductions and repressions being reduced - but not changing sign - which to me would be signs of selection and their absence of would be signs of neutrality - are overlooked. Increasing the resolution would also reveal to what degree selection has acted on clotrimazole inductions and repressions respectively.
Response: Following the reviewer’s recommendation, we have now refined our analysis by dividing the evolved plasticity changes into six categories. Specifically, we first separated genes based on whether their ancestral plasticity in the progenitor represented an induction or a repression under stress. Within each of these two major categories, we further classified the changes observed in the MA lines into three subtypes: strengthened, weakened, and reversed. Here, “strengthened” indicates that the MA line exhibited the same directional response as the progenitor but with a greater magnitude (representing potential non-adaptive plasticity), while “weakened” and “reversed” indicate a loss or reversal of the ancestral response (representing adaptive maintenance of plasticity in the progenitor).
Our results show that for ancestral inductions, expression plasticity in MA lines under clotrimazole exhibited a significantly lower proportion of strengthened changes but significantly higher proportions of weakened and reversed changes compared to the other two stress conditions (Figure below and new Supplementary Figure 3). This pattern suggests that the expression plasticity in clotrimazole is under stronger selective maintenance than plasticity in NaCl or heat stress. A consistent, though less pronounced, trend was observed for ancestral repressions, where clotrimazole again showed a lower proportion of strengthened response and higher proportions of weakened and reversed responses.
Supplementary Figure 3. The proportions of strengthened, weakened, and reversed plasticity for ancestral inductions and suppressions in the MA lines. a, Classification of expression plasticity based on progenitor plasticity (ancestral inductions or suppressions) then classified to strengthened, weakened, and reversed. On the x-axis, ‘O’ represents the expression level in the original environment and ‘P’ represents the expression level in the new environment. Black dots represent the progenitor and orange dots represent MA lines. Pink, purple, and green denote strengthened, weakened, and reversed plasticity, respectively. b, The proportions of strengthened, weakened, and reversed plasticity for ancestral inductions in MA lines across three environments. c, The proportions of strengthened, weakened, and reversed plasticity for ancestral suppressions in MA lines across three environments. In panels b and c, Wilcoxon-test is performed between every two bins with ‘NS.’ represents not significant, ‘*’ represents P < 0.05, and ‘***’ represents P < 0.001.
5. I struggle to accept that gene expression changes induced by NaCl would be selectively neutral, which is implied by the data and alluded to in the text. The NaCl transcriptional response in yeast is well studied, with HOG pathway dependent transcriptional inductions of glycerol production, e.g. via GPD1, and the transcriptional regulation of salt-extrusion via the ENA proteins, being widely accepted as beneficial, selectively favoured responses. A more detailed analysis of what aspects of the NaCl plasticity that are and are not reversed could shed light on what is going on, and form the basis of a more nuanced discussion. The absence of directional changes to NaCl plasticity is almost as surprising as the presence of directional changes to clotrimazole plasticity, and contributes to making it difficult to accept the stringency of the selection test used. Given that only two environments are included, this deserves to be more thoroughly analysed and discussed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and fully understand the concern regarding the apparent neutrality of gene expression plasticity under NaCl stress.
First, to determine whether the neutral pattern observed under NaCl stress is a unique case or represents a general trend for long-standing stressors, we performed an additional experiment examining expression plasticity under heat stress (37 °C), which is another ubiquitous environmental challenge in yeast’s evolutionary history. The results under heat stress closely mirrored those for NaCl. Plastic expression changes showed no consistent directionality across MA lines relative to the progenitor, suggesting that the neutral pattern is not specific to NaCl but may instead represent a general feature of common stressors that yeast have frequently encountered over evolutionary time.
Second, to explain why gene expression plasticity under such common stressors appears neutral at the genome-wide level, we introduced the concept of genetic assimilation in the revised Discussion section. Genetic assimilation, first described by Waddington, refers to the process by which an environmentally induced phenotype becomes genetically fixed, leading to a loss of plasticity over time. This evolutionary mechanism can explain why the initially plastic response has likely been genetically stabilized through recurrent exposure over millions of years.
The following paragraph has been added to the Discussion section to address this point in detail:
“While this conclusion might initially seem counterintuitive, it may be explained by recurrent genetic assimilation. Genetic assimilation, first described by Waddington, occurs when environmentally induced phenotypes (i.e., phenotypic plasticity) become fixed in a population over a few generations, eliminating the need for plasticity18. Later, Lande developed a quantitative-genetic model that demonstrated how a transient increase in phenotypic plasticity, followed by genetic assimilation, can drive adaptation to a novel environment5. The strongest experimental evidence for genetic assimilation comes from a recent study on Silene uniflora36, which has repeatedly adapted to zinc-contaminated soils over the last 250 years. By sequencing the transcriptomes of both zinc-sensitive and zinc-tolerant lineages of Silene uniflora in both zinc-containing and zinc-free environments, researchers identified 183 genes whose plastic expression was fixed in the adapted lineages, providing direct evidence for genetic assimilation. In contrast to the recent 250-year exposure to zinc in Silene uniflora, osmotic and heat stressors in yeast have likely occurred intermittently for millions of years during their evolutionary history. Therefore, much of the adaptive ancestral plastic expression to these stressors may have already been fixed through genetic assimilation. This could explain the neutral pattern of plasticity we observed under NaCl and heat stress.”
Minor issues:
6. The title inappropriately alludes to antibiotics, and is an overreach. Azoles are not antibiotics but antifungals, and this should be corrected throughout the text, and it is an overreach to generalize to “the antibiotic environment” at large, from a single environment. Moreover, I am not sure the authors have shown the majority of individual plastic changes to be beneficial, even in clotrimazole, so predominant is probably not the right word.
Response: The title is now changed to “Contrasting selective signatures of gene expression plasticity in response to antifungal clotrimazole and common environmental stresses in yeast”.
7. Some additional details on the conditions of the MA line evolution would be welcome. The statement that mutations accumulate primarily due to drift comes with an important caveat, as strongly negative mutations are selected against and these constitute a very substantial fraction of the total, in many DFE estimates. The MA conditions would dictate what these strongly negative variants are – for example, if MA conditions contains substantial amounts of Na+, e.g. through setting the pH with NaOH, this would probably influence the NaCl data.
Response: For clarity, the following information have been added to the main text:
“These lines were established using BY4741 as the ancestral strain and underwent approximately 1500 generations of MA in the solid nutrient-rich (YPD) medium at 30 ℃, which lacked the stressors employed in the current study.”
8. NaCl is not only on osmolyte acting externally, as implied in the text, but induces Na+ saline stress intracellularly, e.g. by distorting the Na+/K+ ratio.
Response: For clarity, the following sentence have been added to the main text:
“NaCl induces osmotic stress and distorts intracellular Na+ concentration.”
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This is a review of “Gene expression plasticity in the antibiotic environment is predominantly adaptive in the budding yeast”. Qian et al explore the evolutionary dynamics of phenotypic plasticity in the form of gene expression. MA lines and natural lineages are used to determine if plasticity is adaptive or neutral. They test two stressful conditions - osmotic and antibiotic - and report that gene expression plasticity is adaptive in environments with antifungal but is neutral in osmotic conditions. This conclusion is based on the observation that MA lines, but not natural isolates, lose the ability to adjust their gene expression to environmental change. Thus, the authors conclude that natural selection prevents accumulation of mutations that destroy this ability, while MA experiments do not. We have several major concerns with the way the results are interpreted, and we do not feel that the broad and sweeping conclusions are justified by these data.
Major concern 1: While the experiments address an important question of interest to scientists in many fields, this is not the question discussed in the introduction. The focus of the paper as described in the introduction is the question of whether plasticity allows organisms to persist in a novel environment until a new genetic mutation arises that helps them in that environment. That is an important question, but these results do not pertain to that question. At no point do the authors look for novel genetic mutations occuring and being selected in the stressful environments. They seem to define “adaptive” in the introduction as allowing an organism to persist and survive until it gets a new mutation. In that sense, the authors have not shown plasticity is adaptive at all. This definition of adaptive relates to evolvability. Does plasticity increase evolvability? The experiments have nothing to do with this question and the introduction should be rewritten to focus on the narrower question below.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We agree that our experiments do not directly address whether plasticity facilitates persistence until beneficial mutations arise, which concerns evolvability. Instead, our study focuses on whether gene expression plasticity itself is adaptive, i.e., whether it is selectively maintained by natural selection. To avoid confusion, we have revised the Introduction to clarify this narrower focus.
Specifically, we modified the framing of the research question and added the following sentences to highlight that our study examines the adaptive maintenance of plasticity, not its role in promoting evolvability:
“However, it remains uncertain whether gene expression plasticity is selectively maintained as an adaptive feature or simply represents a transient, non-adaptive response to environmental fluctuations.”
“To address the role of natural selection in the evolution of plasticity under both common and novel stressors…”
Major concern 2: Even when using a more narrow definition of “adaptive”, we still are not sure the results justify the broad sweeping conclusions. When an organism can change its gene expression to match the environment, that likely suggests the organism has previously encountered that environment. That is why gene regulation evolved, to deal with environmental change. So of course, plasticity is adaptive. If plasticity is absent, and an organism cannot change its gene expression to survive an environment, it likely means it never encountered that environment. This ecological perspective, the idea that gene expression regulation reflects an organism's history, is entirely absent from the introduction.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comment and agree that incorporating an ecological and historical perspective on gene regulation is essential for contextualizing the adaptive significance of plasticity. We have revised the Introduction to explicitly discuss how the evolutionary history of environmental exposure shapes the adaptiveness of gene expression plasticity.
Specifically, we added the following new paragraph to the Introduction:
“Moreover, the evolutionary outcomes of plasticity may vary depending on the type of environment encountered, particularly between conditions that have been common throughout an organism’s evolutionary history and those that are novel or rarely experienced. When a stressor has been repeatedly encountered over evolutionary time, such as high salinity (NaCl exposure) or heat stress, organisms are likely to evolve specific adaptive responses to mitigate its effects. Notwithstanding, if such stressors persist over long timescales, plastic responses may eventually become genetically assimilated, resulting in the fixation of adaptive traits and a consequent loss of plasticity5,6,18. In contrast, exposure to novel stressors that were absent from an organism’s evolutionary history poses different challenges. In these cases, organisms may lack specialized adaptive responses but might still cope with stress through mechanisms that overlap with responses to familiar stressors or through broad, general stress-response pathways19.”
Major concern 3: The conclusions appear to relate to all possible drugs and all possible salt environments, while only one of each was studied. Relatedly, the authors only look at two conditions and do not make clear why either was chosen and whether these environments are likely to have been encountered in that past history. The manuscript would benefit from the inclusion of additional environments, particularly more drug conditions. For example, do MA lines consistently show reduced phenotypic plasticity across a range of drug stresses? Without testing other drugs, it’s difficult to support the claim that gene expression plasticity in response to antifungal stress is broadly adaptive, as suggested in the discussion. The same goes for the identified pathways. Perhaps the conclusions could be reframed to emphasize their relevance to clotrimazole specifically. Additionally, the manuscript repeatedly refers to clotrimazole as an "antibiotic," but it is an antifungal which needs to be corrected. Finally, do you think if you tested higher levels of osmotic stress that you would still see a neutral response? Can you please address this in the discussion? Again, I’m not sure these broad generalizations are appropriate based on the tested conditions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive comment. We agree that our original framing was too broad and have revised the manuscript accordingly to clarify the scope and interpretation of our findings.
First, we have reframed the study design and discussion around the comparison between common and novel stressors rather than generalizing across all drugs or all stress conditions. Specifically, NaCl and heat (37 °C) are categorized as common stressors that yeast is likely to have encountered repeatedly throughout their evolutionary history, while clotrimazole is treated as a novel stressor because it is a synthetic antifungal compound developed in the 1960s. We have replaced all instances of “antibiotic” with “antifungal” throughout the manuscript.
To strengthen this comparison, we have now included heat stress as an additional common stressor to test whether the neutral pattern of plasticity under NaCl stress generalizes to another familiar condition. We found that both NaCl and heat stress yielded consistent, largely neutral patterns of expression plasticity, consistent with the hypothesis of genetic assimilation, that ancestral adaptive plasticity to long-standing stressors has been gradually fixed as a stable phenotype (as discussed in the revised Discussion section).
In contrast, expression plasticity under clotrimazole stress showed a clear adaptive pattern, with reduced plasticity and loss of stress-responsive pathways in MA lines relative to the progenitor and natural strains. We have revised the text to explicitly emphasize that this adaptive plasticity pertains specifically to clotrimazole rather than to antifungal or drug stresses in general. Our discussion now focuses on how yeast cells can utilize general stress-response pathways (e.g., oxidative stress response and chemical stimulus response) to cope with novel stressors not encountered in their evolutionary past.
Regarding the environmental relevance of our experimental conditions, we have clarified the rationale for choosing stress intensities that approximate natural conditions for yeast. Specifically, the NaCl concentration used (0.5 M) is comparable to seawater salinity (~0.6 M), and the applied heat stress (37 °C) represents a temperature yeast frequently encounters in natural environments. These choices ensure that the “common stressors” reflect ecologically relevant conditions. However, as the reviewer suggests, applying higher NaCl concentrations or more extreme temperatures would create conditions rarely experienced in nature and might elicit adaptive patterns similar to those observed under clotrimazole stress. We have added a paragraph in the Discussion addressing this possibility and acknowledging that stronger stress levels could alter the observed selective patterns.
Major concern 4: Another concern is that the MA lines used in this study reportedly carry around 900 mutations each which is substantially more than other yeast MA lines, which typically accumulate only a few mutations (see work by Hall lab). Nine hundred is a very high number, and it’s difficult to imagine that all of these mutations truly accumulated in the absence of any selection. It’s well established that lethal mutations do not accumulate in MA experiments. If the salt stress response regulon is essential, it likely would not be mutated, and as a result, you would not observe degradation of plasticity in response to salt. This doesn’t mean plasticity isn’t present—it may simply mean the relevant regulatory pathways were protected from mutation, especially if all media used contained some level of salt. In contrast, the drug condition may have activated a non-essential regulon, which could have been more susceptible to the accumulated mutations. In this way, the experiment may be unintentionally testing for essentiality rather than plasticity.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comment and agree that the relatively high number of accumulated mutations in our MA lines warrants clarification.
In our study, each MA line carries approximately 900 mutations, which is indeed higher than the number typically reported in standard yeast MA experiments. This difference arises because our MA lines were generated in a mutator background (with MSH2 deleted) to accelerate mutation accumulation, followed by restoration of the wild-type MSH2 allele after the MA phase. This approach was adopted deliberately to ensure that sufficient genetic variation accumulated across the genome, thereby increasing the likelihood that mutations would occur in genes or regulatory elements influencing gene expression plasticity. As the reviewer notes, if the MA lines contained too few mutations, the genetic networks underlying plasticity might remain largely untouched, making it difficult to detect any signal of selection. The following paragraph has been added to the Discussion to address the potential influence of MSH2 deletion on the results of our experiment:
“In our MA experiment, we used an MSH2 deletion strain to increase the mutation rate, which also alters the mutational spectrum by elevating the frequency of base substitutions and small insertion–deletion events, particularly in repetitive regions. While this spectrum differs somewhat from that of natural yeast populations, the primary purpose of MA experiments is to allow random mutations to accumulate under minimal selection, thereby gradually eroding the genome. In this sense, even though the precise mutation spectrum may differ, it serves the same functional role as naturally occurring mutations in revealing how random genetic changes affect gene expression and plasticity. Because our analyses focus on the selective patterns acting on these phenotypic outcomes rather than the specific mutation mechanisms, the conclusions regarding the selective maintenance or neutrality of expression plasticity should remain valid.”
We fully agree that lethal mutations cannot accumulate in MA experiments, as such mutations would prevent lineage propagation. However, non-lethal or mildly deleterious mutations can still occur within essential genes if they do not completely abolish gene function. These partial-loss-of-function mutations may still impair regulatory mechanisms related to plasticity without being lethal. To further address the reviewer’s concern that our observed patterns might reflect differences in essentiality rather than plasticity, we compared the proportions of essential genes among DEGs responding to NaCl, heat, and clotrimazole in the progenitor strain. We agree that essential stress-response regulons are less likely to accumulate disruptive mutations, and this may indeed explain the relative stability of NaCl/heat plasticity compared with clotrimazole. However, we found that the proportion of essential genes among clotrimazole-responsive DEGs was significantly higher than that in NaCl or heat responses (χ² test, P < 0.01). This result suggests that the antifungal stress response involves a larger number of essential or core cellular functions, rather than a more dispensable regulon. Therefore, our findings are unlikely to be explained solely by differences in essentiality between stress responses.
Major concern 5: The figures, as currently presented, are not effective in highlighting the key findings and in many cases feel redundant.

The phylogenetic trees might be better placed in the supplement. Additionally, the natural strain names used here are inconsistent with those used elsewhere in the paper. If phylogenetic trees are included, the best-fit model and root should be reported.
d) Consider combining these panels into a single plot for clarity.

Supplemental Figures:
Supplemental Figure 4 appears to be identical to panels b–e from the main text, including the figure legend. If this is the case, it should either be removed or clearly justified.

Panel (a) presents a schematic overview of the experimental design and analytical workflow, which helps readers quickly grasp the logic of the study. The TVM substitution model was applied, as determined by model selection within IQ-TREE.”
Regarding the reviewer’s point that BY4741 under clotrimazole clusters with natural strains rather than MA lines, we agree that this is an interesting and important pattern. In fact, this pattern is indeed consistent with our key conclusion: expression profiles under clotrimazole stress are adaptively maintained. The clustering indicates that the progenitor (BY4741) and natural strains share conserved adaptive transcriptional responses that were largely lost in the MA lines, reflecting the selective maintenance of plasticity in the antifungal environment. We have now explicitly discussed this interpretation in the revised manuscript (Discussion section, lines 364-368).

Minor concern 1: The use of bulk RNAseq in this study feels somewhat outdated, especially given the availability of single-cell RNAseq methods. Bulk approaches average expression across thousands of cells, potentially masking meaningful cell-to-cell variation that could be critical for understanding plasticity. Gene expression plasticity may not be uniform across a population—some subpopulations may respond strongly while others do not, and this heterogeneity can be biologically important. Incorporating single-cell methods could provide deeper insight into the dynamics and distribution of plastic responses, particularly under stress conditions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We fully agree that single-cell RNAseq offers powerful opportunities to explore cell-to-cell variation in gene expression. However, our study focuses on population-level transcriptional plasticity and on comparisons among multiple strains and MA lines across several environments. In this context, bulk RNAseq provides an established and appropriate approach for quantifying average gene expression responses at the population level. We noted that many recent studies addressing gene expression plasticity and its evolution (PMID: 26331546 and PMID: 36702857) have successfully used bulk RNA-seq to characterize environmentally induced transcriptional changes. Following this well-established framework ensures comparability with previous work and allows robust inference of plasticity at the transcriptome scale.
Minor concern 2: There were several typos throughout the manuscript. A thorough re-read and careful editing are strongly recommended. Additionally, the inclusion of line numbers would have made it easier to provide specific, targeted feedback.
Response: We have thoroughly proofread the manuscript and corrected typographical and grammatical errors throughout. In addition, line numbers have been added to the submitted manuscript.

Reviewer #2:
I remain appreciative of this submission. The idea of using the directionality of changes to plastic responses during forced neutral evolution is original and fundamentally sound. I still I am still not convinced about some of the interpretations, as detailed below.
The main issue, to me, is that the authors have no unquestionable positive control to validate their method and ensure that it captures true instances of historical natural selection on phenotypic plasticity. To me, the ideal positive controls would have been the plasticity associated with the key life history transitions in yeast, from stationary phase to growth, the diauxic shift, sporulation, or germination – key aspects of these are certainly established by natural selection. The absence of an excellent positive control leaves the paper open to criticism.
That said, I think the authors have gone to substantial lengths to alleviate my concerns. Therefore, and given the refreshing originality of the idea, I would recommend publication given that the below is addressed.
Necessary revisions:
1. The growth curves supplied to ensure that there are no differences in physiological state between MA and progenitor must be on log-scale. Unless curves are on a log-scale, the existence and length of an exponential phase remain unclear. If MA lines e.g. in clotrimazole have begun experiencing energy restrictions at the time of sampling, while the progenitor has not, there will be a systematic difference in gene expression that could bias results and potentially generate the clotrimazole trends. The truly convincing way to exclude this would be to show the derivatives of growth curves with exact sampling times indicated. If MA and progenitor cells are not in the same phase, this needs to be highlighted and discussed as a caveat.
Response: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. Following your recommendation, we have added a new supplementary figure 9 showing the derivatives of the growth curves (dOD/dt) with sampling times indicated. To generate these, we subtracted the background OD (~0.1) from raw readings and calculated growth rates as time derivatives of OD based on 20-min intervals from the plate reader. The resulting dOD/dt values were plotted against OD, with the sampling window (OD = 0.4–0.6) highlighted in grey. Because growth follows a logistic trajectory, we applied quadratic smoothing to reduce noise in the derivative estimates. These analyses confirm that all samples were collected during the exponential phase and that MA lines and the progenitor were in comparable physiological states at the time of sampling.

The gray shaded areas indicate the sampling windows. To calculate the derivatives, the background OD (~0.1) was subtracted from the raw readings, and growth rates were computed as time derivatives of OD based on 20-minute intervals from the plate reader. Given the logistic nature of growth, quadratic smoothing was applied to reduce noise in the derivative estimates.
2. I am not at all convinced about the genetic assimilation argument. The yeast literature on NaCl plastic responses is very rich, and gives us a very solid base for evaluating such claims. From this literature, it seems quite clear to me that S. cerevisiae is not innately salt tolerant and has not genetically assimilated an original plastic response that since then has become obsolete. In contrast, it seems quite clear that plastic inductions of ENA1 and/or GPD1 remain absolutely critical for negotiating a period of elevated NaCl exposure in extant yeasts. Non-redundant genes involved in the plastic induction of ENA1 and/or GPD1 are critical for salt tolerance, as are ENA1 and either of GPD1/GPD2. A few other regulations also appear somewhat important, e.g. of NHA1. So – the key aspects of the plastic response to salt have not been genetically assimilated. The authors could instead argue that ENA1 and GPD1 inductions represent a small fraction of the many gene expression changes that occur during salt exposure – and that the overall response, considering the total number of regulations, is neutral. To me, that would amount to saying that as long as ENA1 and GPD1 and maybe NHA1 is induced, it doesn’t matter much what other gene expression changes occur – and that selection hasn’t acted on optimizing the plastic responses to NaCl beyond ensuring that the key inductions are achieved and weeding out any too costly unnecessary inductions/repressions. From a simple counting perspective, the few beneficial changes would then drown in the hundreds of neutral expression variations. In fact, the lack of overall correlation between what genes are important and what genes are induced during NaCl exposure https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14676322/ could be interpreted in this way. A discussion along these lines might add nuance and depth to how we see gene expression plasticity, but the authors should refrain from giving the false impression that the entire salt response is neutral, or genetically assimilated. I am not sure whether the heat response is sufficiently well understood for the same reasoning to hold.

We fully agree that S. cerevisiae’s salt tolerance depends critically on plastic induction of ENA1, GPD1/GPD2, and NHA1, and that these pathways have not been genetically assimilated. Our intention was not to imply that the entire NaCl response is genetically fixed. Rather, our data indicate that, at the transcriptome-wide level, gene expression plasticity under NaCl stress shows a random distribution across MA lines (consistent with neutrality in most genes) while specific components (such as ENA1 and GPD1) remain functionally indispensable and adaptively plastic.
To address, we have revised the manuscript to more clearly distinguish between the adaptive core and the broader neutral response. Specifically, we emphasize that the canonical osmoadaptive modules, including the HOG pathway, ENA1, and GPD1/GPD2, remain actively induced and are under strong selective constraint. The apparent neutrality we report pertains to the global pattern of transcriptional plasticity, where many expression changes appear to be selectively unconstrained or evolve in a neutral manner. We suggest that selection maintains only the essential subset of plastic responses required for salt tolerance, while many peripheral expression changes are effectively neutral or reflect relaxed optimization, as the reviewer points out.
In light of these revisions, we have added the following paragraph to the Discussion section:
While our study primarily focused on the overall pattern of plastic expression, we acknowledge that certain genes may still exhibit adaptive plasticity under NaCl stress. For example, the core osmoadaptive modules, particularly the HOG pathway, ENA1, and GPD1/GPD2, remain essential and show strong, adaptive induction in response to NaCl stress (Gasch et al., 2000; Warringer et al., 2003). However, our data suggest that beyond this essential core, the broader pattern of transcriptome-wide plastic expression changes appears largely random across MA lines, which is consistent with neutral variation in many genes. This observation indicates that while selection continues to preserve the critical plastic responses needed for osmotic balance and ion homeostasis, many peripheral transcriptional responses may evolve under relaxed selection or drift. In this way, adaptive plasticity is maintained where it is functionally necessary, but the entire stress-responsive network is not globally optimized.
Minor issues.
1. It is not correct to say that YPD lacks Na+. There is no added NaCl, but the yeast extract and peptones do contain the ions, in varying amounts depending on batch. The batch variations is one reason to use SC instead of YPD.
Response: Thank you for your valuable feedback. We have reviewed the documentation for the chemicals, including peptone and yeast extract, used in the MA experiment. According to the Certificates of Analysis for these materials:
https://documents.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/certificate/MN/COA/COA_LP0037B_11042025030433_6208751_1.pdf
https://documents.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/BPD/certificate/Certificate-of-Analysis/212720%20-%203257238.pdf
On average, peptone and yeast extract contain about 0.3% sodium chloride, resulting in a final sodium chloride concentration of approximately 0.012% in YPD medium. In comparison, the sodium chloride concentration in 0.5 M NaCl is 2.92%, which is more than two hundred times higher. Given this substantial difference, we determined that the amount of sodium chloride from peptone and yeast extract would have a minimal impact on our experiment. However, we will remain mindful that YPD does contain trace amounts of ions, which could influence future experiments.
2. The protocol for growth rate estimations appears not to be from ref 44 but from
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14676322/?
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. You are correct that our growth rate estimation protocol follows the method described by Warringer et al. (2003; PMID: 14676322). We have now cited both this paper and our previously listed reference (ref. 44) to accurately acknowledge the original source of the method.
Reviewer #3:
In this revised version, the authors have responded thoroughly and constructively to our earlier concerns. They substantially revised the Introduction to focus on the question their data directly address, namely whether gene expression plasticity is selectively maintained rather than its role in evolvability. They also added important ecological and historical context by explicitly distinguishing between common and novel stressors and by invoking genetic assimilation for long-standing stresses. The scope of the conclusions has been appropriately narrowed to clotrimazole and to general stress-response mechanisms, rather than to antibiotics or drugs broadly, and terminology has been corrected throughout. Several concerns about potential technical and experimental artefacts have been alleviated by the inclusion of new growth-curve data, additional heat-stress experiments, refined analyses of plasticity categories, and competitive fitness assays in clotrimazole and hydrogen peroxide that link loss of plasticity to reduced fitness in relevant environments. The authors have also clarified the consequences of using an MSH2 mutator background, addressed the issue of essentiality, and improved the clarity and organization of the figures, including better integration of the natural strains. While the interpretation of adaptive plasticity may still depend on perspective, the main conclusions are now well supported by the data, and we are satisfied that major concerns have been adequately addressed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their positive and constructive feedback. We are pleased that the revisions have addressed the earlier concerns and that the main conclusions are now considered well supported.

Non-redundant genes involved in the plastic induction of ENA1 and/or GPD1 are critical for salt tolerance, as are ENA1 and either of GPD1/GPD2. A few other regulations also appear somewhat important, e.g. of NHA1. So – the key aspects of the plastic response to salt have not been genetically assimilated. The authors could instead argue that ENA1 and GPD1 inductions represent a small fraction of the many gene expression changes that occur during salt exposure – and that the overall response, considering the total number of regulations, is neutral. To me, that would amount to saying that as long as ENA1 and GPD1 and maybe NHA1 is induced, it doesn’t matter much what other gene expression changes occur – and that selection hasn’t acted on optimizing the plastic responses to NaCl beyond ensuring that the key inductions are achieved and weeding out any too costly unnecessary inductions/repressions. From a simple counting perspective, the few beneficial changes would then drown in the hundreds of neutral expression variations. In fact, the lack of overall correlation between what genes are important and what genes are induced during NaCl exposure https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14676322/ could be interpreted in this way. A discussion along these lines might add nuance and depth to how we see gene expression plasticity, but the authors should refrain from giving the false impression that the entire salt response is neutral, or genetically assimilated. I am not sure whether the heat response is sufficiently well understood for the same reasoning to hold.
Minor issues.
1. It is not correct to say that YPD lacks Na+. There is no added NaCl, but the yeast extract and peptones do contain the ions, in varying amounts depending on batch. The batch variations is one reason to use SC instead of YPD.
2. The protocol for growth rate estimations appears not to be from ref 44 but from
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14676322/?

### Reviewer 3

In this revised version, the authors have responded thoroughly and constructively to our earlier concerns. They substantially revised the Introduction to focus on the question their data directly address, namely whether gene expression plasticity is selectively maintained rather than its role in evolvability. They also added important ecological and historical context by explicitly distinguishing between common and novel stressors and by invoking genetic assimilation for long-standing stresses. The scope of the conclusions has been appropriately narrowed to clotrimazole and to general stress-response mechanisms, rather than to antibiotics or drugs broadly, and terminology has been corrected throughout.
Several concerns about potential technical and experimental artefacts have been alleviated by the inclusion of new growth-curve data, additional heat-stress experiments, refined analyses of plasticity categories, and competitive fitness assays in clotrimazole and hydrogen peroxide that link loss of plasticity to reduced fitness in relevant environments. The authors have also clarified the consequences of using an MSH2 mutator background, addressed the issue of essentiality, and improved the clarity and organization of the figures, including better integration of the natural strains. While the interpretation of adaptive plasticity may still depend on perspective, the main conclusions are now well supported by the data, and we are satisfied that major concerns have been adequately addressed.
